individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper introduces CodeAlignBench, a benchmark for evaluating instruction-following in code generation. It collects real developer instructions via a user study across Python, Java, and JavaScript, categorizes them into cosmetic, structural, and semantic types, and builds an automated framework using rule-based and LLM-judge functions to check instruction applicability and adherence. The authors evaluate 10 commercial LLMs on LiveBench tasks translated into three languages under two settings (predefined and follow-up instructions), reporting that follow-up tasks are easier, structural instructions are best followed, GPT models lead, and no model saturates. They also assess LLM judge reliability against human consensus with ~87% agreement.
Strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored dimension of code generation evaluation: adherence to developer preferences beyond functional correctness.
Grounds instruction categories in real developer preferences through a user study, rather than using only synthetic constraints.
The modular design with is_applicable and verify functions is extensible to other standalone coding problems and instruction types.
Provides a multi-language evaluation (Python, Java, JavaScript) and demonstrates effort to extend a live benchmark.
Includes statistical tests (Wilcoxon, Friedman) to support observed differences and a preliminary LLM-judge reliability check.
Weaknesses: The paper is incomplete and has unclear presentation: Table 1 is confusing, references are duplicated, and several methodological details (e.g., value of k, exact prompts, translation validation) are missing or deferred to supplementary materials.

The user study is small and may not be representative: only 10 raters per language, all from competitive programming tasks, with no evidence that the instruction catalog covers realistic developer workflows.
The automated translation pipeline from Python to Java/JavaScript is not evaluated; errors in translation could undermine cross-language comparisons.

LLM judge reliability is assessed on only 30 instructions, yielding 86.7% accuracy with a large uncertainty; there is no per-category or per-language breakdown, and no comparison to rule-based verifiers on the same tasks.
The benchmark is evaluated only on proprietary LLMs; no open-source models are included, limiting reproducibility and community use.

The claim of being 'the first' IF benchmark for real-world developer instructions is overstated given prior work like CodeIF-Bench and CodeUltraFeedback, which also address instruction following and code preferences.

The Applicability Checker sampling procedure is underspecified: the number k and how generic instructions are selected for each code sample are not defined, affecting the validity of task construction.
Questions: What is the exact value of k (number of applicable instructions sampled per code snippet), and how is it chosen?
How was the Python-to-Java/JavaScript translation validated? What is the pass rate of translated solutions on original test cases?
What are the exact prompts used for LLM-assisted coding and LLM judging? Are they included in the supplementary materials?
What is the confidence interval for the 86.7% human agreement rate, and how many instructions were from each category and language?
Were any open-source models (e.g., CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder) evaluated? If not, why not?
How were 'no preference' responses handled in the user study, and how many were there?
Did the authors consider combining multiple instructions per task, despite claiming this as future work?
Limitations: The instruction catalog is limited in size (228 verified instructions) and heavily imbalanced across categories, with only 32 cosmetic vs. 114 structural.
The evaluation relies on competitive programming problems, which may not reflect real-world code bases and developer preferences.
The LLM judge used for verification may carry model-specific bias; the ablation only covers two models and two languages.
Binary success metrics may not capture partial adherence or nuanced instruction following.
No public release of code or data is provided in the paper, hindering reproducibility.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper introduces CodeAlignBench, a multi-language benchmark for evaluating instruction-following in code generation. It collects developer-authored code refinement instructions via a user study, organizes them into a taxonomy (cosmetic, structural, semantic with subcategories), and provides an automated pipeline that constructs instruction-following tasks from existing coding problems (LiveBench) and verifies adherence using rule-based or LLM-as-a-judge methods. The authors evaluate 10 LLMs in two settings (predefined and follow-up instructions) across Python, Java, and JavaScript, finding that models perform better on follow-up tasks, structural instructions are easiest, and GPT-5-family models lead. They also report an LLM-judge human agreement of 86.7%.
Strengths: Novel user-study-driven collection of real-world developer instruction preferences across three programming languages, leading to a taxonomy of instruction types (cosmetic, structural, semantic).
Extensible pipeline design with is_applicable and verify interfaces, supporting both rule-based and LLM-based checking, and applicable to any set of standalone coding problems.
Multi-language evaluation by extending LiveBench from Python to Java and JavaScript, with an automated translation pipeline.
Evaluation of both predefined and follow-up instruction settings, revealing meaningful performance differences and a model ranking distinct from functional correctness.
Validation of the LLM judge against human judgments (86.7% agreement) and an ablation for judge bias, albeit partial.
Weaknesses: Multiple numerical inconsistencies: the paper states 250 responses for manual coding though 50 per language sums to 150; instruction totals are 32+89+114=235 but reported as 228, and Table 1 lists 104 structural vs 114 in text; model names are inconsistent (e.g., GPT-5 Nano vs GPT o4 mini vs GPT o3 mini).

Insufficient experimental details: the number of base tasks per language, the value of k for applicable instructions per task, the number of IF tasks per category, and the exact sampling procedure for tasks and instructions are not specified.
The translation pipeline from Python to Java/JavaScript is described only vaguely, with no validation of translation correctness or human review reported.
LLM judge reliability is assessed on only 30 instructions, and no per-category or rule-based verifier accuracy is provided; the abstract's claim of averaging 87% may be overgeneralized.
Statistical tests are reported without key details such as sample sizes, exact task counts, or multiple-comparison corrections; wide confidence intervals suggest small sample sizes.

The claim of being the 'first' benchmark for real-world developer instruction following is not fully supported given existing benchmarks like CodeIF-Bench and BigCodeBench-Instruct, which are discussed but whose differences are not sharply delineated.
The implementations of is_applicable and verify are only in supplementary materials, making it difficult to assess their robustness or reproduce the benchmark without those details.
Questions: How many LiveBench coding problems are used per language, and how many IF tasks are generated per problem and per instruction category?
What is the value of k (number of applicable instructions per task)? How is k chosen and balanced across categories and types?
How was the automated translation from Python to Java and JavaScript validated? What is the correctness rate of the translated code and test cases?
Can the authors reconcile the discrepancy in the user study sample size (50 per language vs 250 total) and the instruction totals (32+89+114=235 vs 228, and Table 1's 104 structural)?
How were the 30 instructions for LLM judge validation selected, and is an 86.7% agreement rate statistically robust given the small sample?
What were the exact sample sizes for the Wilcoxon and Friedman tests, and were corrections for multiple comparisons applied?
The paper refers to 'GPT-5 Nano' and 'GPT o4 mini' in different sections; are these the same as 'GPT-5 mini' and 'GPT o3 mini' in Table 2? Please use consistent model names.
Limitations: The benchmark is built only on competitive programming tasks (LeetCode/AtCoder), which may not represent real-world repository-level software engineering.
The instruction catalog may not be complete, and generic instructions derived from category descriptions may not fully capture the specificity of original developer feedback.
The LLM judge used for verification (Claude Sonnet 4) may introduce bias, and the ablation covers only JavaScript/Java with GPT-5 as judge, not all languages and models.
The human raters (10 per language) are relatively few, and subjective preferences may vary across developers, limiting the generalizability of the instruction taxonomy.
The translation pipeline could introduce language-specific errors, and no human validation of translated tasks is reported.
No public release or URL for the benchmark code/data is mentioned; the paper only says supplementary materials are provided.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper introduces CodeAlignBench, a benchmark and automated pipeline for evaluating instruction-following in code generation. It collects developer preferences/instructions via a user study across Python, Java, and JavaScript, organizes them into a taxonomy (cosmetic, structural, semantic), and provides an extensible framework with is_applicable/verify functions to construct tasks from any standalone coding problems (using LiveBench). It evaluates 10 LLMs in two settings (predefined and follow-up instructions), showing differences across languages/categories, and reports LLM-judge agreement around 87%.
Strengths: Real-world grounding: instructions are collected from 30 developers via pairwise code preference tasks, rather than synthetic constraints, and organized through an LLM-assisted coding process into a taxonomy.
Extensible modular framework: the is_applicable/verify interface allows new problems/instructions to be added and supports mixed rule-based and LLM-judge checks.
Multi-language evaluation: automatically translated LiveBench tasks into Java and JavaScript, enabling cross-language comparisons beyond Python-only benchmarks.
Thorough empirical analysis of 10 models, with statistical tests and a judge-bias ablation showing relative rankings are stable across judges.
Contamination mitigation through using continuously updated LiveBench tasks, addressing a known limitation of static benchmarks.
Weaknesses: Functional correctness is not checked after applying instructions: the verify function only checks whether the instruction was followed, so a model could be rewarded for producing code that follows style/structure but is semantically wrong; the benchmark does not report whether updated code still passes tests.

The LLM-judge reliability validation is weak: it is based on only 30 curated instructions with author consensus labels (86.67% agreement), not a large or independent sample; per-instruction verifier accuracy is not reported.

Applicability and verification implementations are mostly deferred to supplementary material; the main text does not specify the exact rule-based or LLM prompts for each instruction type, making reproducibility hard to assess.
The Java/JavaScript translation pipeline is described only briefly, with no validation of how often translated problems remain faithful and correctly functioning across languages.

The benchmark is limited to short algorithmic competitive-programming tasks; instructions such as refactoring, dependency management, or repository-level concerns are not covered, so it remains unclear how well results transfer to real-world codebases.

The user study instruction catalog is relatively small (228 verified instructions) and language-specific instructions are uneven; semantic categories include only six correctness instructions, limiting conclusions about correctness-related instruction following.
Questions: How many LiveBench problems are used per language, and what is the total number of generated IF tasks per setting/category? The reported confidence intervals suggest small samples; exact counts are needed to assess statistical power.
Does the evaluation ensure the updated code still passes the original test cases? If not, what proportion of model responses that satisfy the instruction are functionally incorrect?
For predefined-instruction tasks, how is applicability of an instruction determined? Is the instruction applied to the problem statement or to the model's initial (unconstrained) solution?
Can the authors provide the complete list of is_applicable/verify implementations and prompts for all instruction IDs? Without these, independent replication is not possible.
How was the Java/JavaScript automatic translation validated? Were translated problems executed and checked for equivalence to the original Python problems, and what was the pass rate?

How many instructions per category were actually used in the final benchmark after filtering for generic applicability? For example, only six 'correctness' instructions exist—how many sampled tasks involved correctness?
Limitations: The benchmark's instruction catalog is derived from a small set of developers and competitive programming tasks, which may not represent the diversity of real-world developer preferences.
The pipeline does not currently incorporate multi-turn iterative refinement or combined instructions, despite being mentioned as future work.
LLM-as-a-judge verification may exhibit systematic biases that are not fully controlled; the judge-bias ablation only covers two languages and two judges.
No analysis is provided for the reliability of the applicability checker, which may propagate errors to task construction.
Potential human-subject considerations in the user study are not discussed (e.g., consent, IRB).

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper introduces CodeAlignBench, a benchmark for evaluating how well LLMs follow developer instructions during code generation. Instructions are collected from a user study with 30 developers across Python, Java, and JavaScript, then organized into a taxonomy (cosmetic, structural, semantic including algorithm, performance, correctness). An automated pipeline constructs instruction-following tasks from LiveBench coding problems (with automatic translation to Java and JavaScript) and evaluates models in two settings: predefined instructions embedded in the initial prompt and follow-up instructions after an initial generation. The authors evaluate 10 models from OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini families, report that models generally perform better on follow-up tasks, and find significant gaps across instruction categories and languages.
Strengths: The benchmark is grounded in a real user study: 30 developers with 3-16 years of experience provided 228 verified instructions, making the evaluation more ecologically valid than purely synthetic instruction benchmarks.
The modular pipeline with is_applicable and verify interfaces supports both rule-based and LLM-judge implementations, making it extensible to new problems, instructions, and languages.
The two settings (predefined vs. follow-up) provide a useful decomposition of instruction-following ability, and the finding that follow-up tasks are consistently easier is actionable.
The paper includes an ablation with an alternative judge (GPT-5) to assess judge bias, showing that relative model rankings remain mostly consistent across judge choices.
Using LiveBench tasks helps reduce the risk of data contamination compared to static benchmarks.
Weaknesses: The claim of being the 'first IF benchmark' for code is overstated given existing work such as CodeIF-Bench and BigCodeBench-Instruct, which also evaluate instruction following in code generation.

The LLM judge validation is based on only 30 instructions (86.67% accuracy), which is a small and potentially non-representative sample; the abstract's 'averaging 87%' is not clearly tied to a consistent evaluation protocol.

The implementations of is_applicable and verify are not described in the paper; all details are deferred to supplementary, making it difficult for an expert to reproduce the benchmark without external materials.

The statistical analysis appears incomplete: Friedman tests are reported without post-hoc pairwise comparisons, multiple comparisons are not corrected, and some key findings (e.g., Java structural category) are not significant, yet the paper draws strong conclusions.

The Python-to-Java/JavaScript translation pipeline is not validated by human experts or additional tests, so quality and semantic equivalence of translated problems remain unclear, which could confound cross-language comparisons.
The paper does not report the number of tasks per language and instruction category, leaving sample sizes and the statistical power of the reported results unclear.

Several model names (e.g., GPT-5, GPT-5 mini, GPT o4 mini, GPT 5 Nano, Claude Sonnet 4) do not match publicly known model names at the time of review; this raises reproducibility concerns unless exact API versions are specified.
Questions: How many IF tasks were constructed per language and per instruction category, and what are the exact sample sizes behind the scores in Table 2?
Can you provide a complete worked example of is_applicable and verify for at least one instruction category, including whether it is rule-based, LLM-judge, or hybrid?
Was the automatic translation from Python to Java and JavaScript validated by human annotators or by checking semantic equivalence on additional test sets beyond LiveBench hidden tests?
What is the inter-rater reliability of the LLM judge on a larger, more diverse set of instructions, and are the observed score differences robust to judge choice with statistical significance?
How were the 30 verification instructions selected for the LLM-judge reliability evaluation, and were they balanced across languages, categories, and difficulty?
Are the GPT-5, GPT-5 mini, GPT o4 mini, and GPT 5 Nano models public releases or proprietary API models? If so, what exact versions and access dates were used?
Limitations: The verifier reliability is assessed on only 30 instructions, which is too small to establish high confidence in automated evaluation at scale.
The use of a single LLM judge (Claude Sonnet 4) for many verifications may introduce systematic bias that is not fully mitigated by the limited GPT-5 ablation.
The automatic translation pipeline may introduce subtle semantic errors in Java and JavaScript, undermining the validity of cross-language comparisons.
The instruction taxonomy is coarse and may have overlapping categories (e.g., performance vs. algorithm), making it difficult to attribute model failures to a specific type.

The paper does not report the number of LiveBench problems used, how many were successfully translated, or how many passed applicability checks, so benchmark coverage and task difficulty are not transparent.
The user-study instructions are public and may eventually appear in model training corpora, potentially leading to contamination over time despite the use of LiveBench.

review.Summary: The paper introduces CodeAlignBench, a benchmark and pipeline for evaluating instruction-following in LLM code generation. It collects real developer instructions via a user study with 30 developers across Python, Java, and JavaScript, organizes them into a taxonomy (cosmetic, structural, semantic), and builds an automated framework that checks instruction applicability and verifies instruction adherence using rule-based methods and LLM judges. The benchmark is evaluated on 10 LLMs using tasks from LiveBench, extended to Java and JavaScript via automated translation, under both predefined-instruction and follow-up-instruction settings. Results show models perform better on follow-up tasks than predefined tasks, structural instructions are easiest, and top models still leave room for improvement on semantic and cosmetic categories.
Strengths: Addresses a meaningful gap in code generation evaluation by moving beyond functional correctness to developer-defined instruction adherence, grounded in a user study rather than synthetic tasks.
The modular pipeline with is_applicable and verify functions is extensible to new problem sets and languages, and the multi-language extension from Python to Java/JavaScript is useful.

The empirical evaluation covers 10 models from multiple families across two instruction settings and three instruction categories, revealing non-obvious trends such as follow-up tasks being easier and structural instructions being best followed.
Includes human agreement checks for LLM-based verification and an ablation on judge bias, which strengthens confidence in the evaluation methodology.
Weaknesses: The paper contains serious internal inconsistencies in reported counts: Section 2.2 says 50 responses per language but then refers to 250 responses (should be 150); Table 1 lists 184 Java, 175 JavaScript, 171 Python instructions, yet the total is stated as 228; the category counts (32+89+104=225) do not equal 228, and the text says 114 structural instructions while Table 1 says 104.

The predefined-instruction setting is described inconsistently: Section 3.2 says 'providing the coding problem with only the instruction,' while earlier sections and Figure 1 describe the instruction being embedded in the initial prompt along with the problem; this ambiguity affects the interpretation of the experimental comparison.

The evaluation framework lacks critical implementation details: exact prompts for predefined vs. follow-up settings, the number of IF tasks generated per language, how instructions are sampled per code sample, and concrete implementations of is_applicable/verify functions are not described in the main text, hurting reproducibility.

LLM judge reliability is validated on only 30 instructions (86.7% agreement, 4 disagreements), which is a very small sample and insufficient to support the abstract's claim of 'averaging 87%' reliability; no confidence intervals or per-category reliability are provided.

The claim of being 'the first IF benchmark' for this setting is contradicted by the related work section itself, which cites CodeIF-Bench, BigCodeBench-Instruct, and CodeUltraFeedback as prior benchmarks for instruction-following or code preferences.
The automated translation from Python to Java/JavaScript is not validated for semantic equivalence or quality, so cross-language comparisons may be confounded by translation errors.
Questions: How many IF tasks were constructed in total per language and per setting (predefined/follow-up), and what is the distribution of instruction categories in the evaluated tasks?

Can you clarify the exact prompt format for the predefined setting: does the model receive the problem statement plus a generic instruction, and if so, how does this differ from the follow-up setting beyond the presence of initial code?

For each instruction category, what specific rule-based or LLM-judge prompts were used in is_applicable and verify? Could these be included in the appendix or supplementary material in a way that enables exact reproduction?
How was the balanced sampling of code generations implemented in the user study, and how many developer responses were collected and retained after the consistency check?
Why are the counts in Table 1 inconsistent with the total and with the text (e.g., Java+JS+Python vs. total, category sums, and 104 vs. 114 structural instructions)? Please provide corrected numbers.
What is the statistical power of the model comparisons given the number of tasks, and were corrections for multiple comparisons applied in the Friedman/Wilcoxon tests?
Limitations: The user study and benchmark tasks are derived from competitive programming problems (LeetCode/AtCoder), so the instruction catalog may not reflect the complexity or type of instructions found in real-world, repository-scale software development.
The benchmark relies on LLM-as-a-judge for instruction verification, which is imperfect and potentially biased toward certain model families; the human validation is too limited to fully assess this.
The automatically translated Java and JavaScript versions of LiveBench tasks are not validated for quality or semantic equivalence, which limits the reliability of cross-language conclusions.

The evaluation does not cover multi-turn or combined-instruction scenarios, although the paper mentions them as future work, leaving a gap between the benchmark's potential and its current empirical scope.
Potential social or ethical impacts are not discussed; the paper also does not mention whether the user study received IRB approval or informed consent.

review.Summary: The paper introduces CodeAlignBench, a benchmark for evaluating instruction-following in code generation. It collects real developer instructions via a user study across Python, Java, and JavaScript, categorizes them into cosmetic, structural, and semantic types, and provides an automated framework with applicability checks and rule-based/LLM-based verification. The authors evaluate 10 proprietary LLMs on LiveBench tasks translated to three languages under predefined and follow-up instruction settings, finding that follow-up tasks are easier, structural instructions are best followed, and no model saturates. They also report LLM judge reliability at ~87% human agreement.
Strengths: Grounded in a real user study with 30 developers, providing ecologically valid developer instructions rather than synthetic constraints.
Modular pipeline design (is_applicable/verify) is extensible to other standalone coding problems, languages, and instruction types.
Multi-language evaluation (Python, Java, JavaScript) via automated translation extends beyond Python-only benchmarks.
Both predefined and follow-up instruction settings offer a useful decomposition of instruction-following ability.
Includes statistical tests and an LLM-judge bias ablation, showing relative model rankings are somewhat stable across judges.
Weaknesses: Multiple internal inconsistencies in reported counts (user study sample size, instruction totals, category numbers) and inconsistent model names across text and tables.
Insufficient methodological details: exact number of tasks, value of k, sampling procedures, and full implementations of is_applicable/verify are deferred to supplementary, hampering reproducibility.
LLM judge reliability is validated on only 30 instructions; 86.7% agreement has high uncertainty, and no per-category or per-language breakdown is provided.
Automated Python-to-Java/JavaScript translation is not validated for semantic equivalence, threatening the validity of cross-language comparisons.
Claims of being the 'first' benchmark for real-world developer instruction-following are overstated given prior work such as CodeIF-Bench and BigCodeBench-Instruct.
Evaluation is limited to proprietary LLMs; no open-source models are included, limiting reproducibility and community use.
Questions: How many LiveBench problems are used per language, and what is the total number of generated IF tasks per setting and category?
What is the exact value of k (number of applicable instructions sampled per problem) and how is it chosen?
How was the Python-to-Java/JavaScript translation validated? What is the correctness rate of translated solutions on original test cases?
What are the exact prompts used for LLM-assisted coding and LLM-jude verification? Are they fully included in the supplementary materials?
How were the 30 instructions for LLM-judge validation selected, and what is the confidence interval for the 86.7% agreement rate?
Why do the counts in Table 1 not match the text totals (e.g., 228 vs 235, 104 vs 114 structural instructions)?
Were any open-source models (e.g., CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder) evaluated? If not, why?
How were 'no preference' responses handled in the user study, and how many were there?
Limitations: Instruction catalog is small (228 verified) and derived from competitive programming tasks, which may not represent real-world, repository-level software development.
LLM-as-a-judge verification may carry systematic model-specific bias; the bias ablation covers only two languages and two judge models.
Automated translation errors could confound cross-language comparisons, and no human validation of translated tasks is reported.
Binary success metrics may not capture partial instruction adherence or nuanced quality.
No public release of code or data is mentioned in the paper, hindering reproducibility.
Potential ethical considerations for the user study (e.g., informed consent, IRB approval) are not discussed.
